sections.h2: Where is Charlottesville, VA, and how does it relate to Albemarle County?
sections.html:
Charlottesville is an independent city in central Virginia, on rolling hills along the Rivanna River just west of the Southwest Mountains. It is the county seat of Albemarle County, which surrounds the city on all sides, yet the two are separate governments.

The city covers about 10.3 square miles and sits roughly 99 miles from Washington, D.C. and 72 miles from Richmond. The 2020 census counted 46,553 residents, and the Census Bureau's 2025 estimate is 44,388. The wider Charlottesville metro area, which takes in Albemarle, Fluvanna, Greene and Nelson counties, has about 221,524 people.

That city-versus-county line is the first thing to check when you plan a sale. A house with a Charlottesville mailing address may be in Albemarle County, and the tax office, permit office and zoning rules differ depending on which side of the line your parcel is on. Most of the University of Virginia's grounds, for example, are legally in Albemarle County even though they feel like part of the city.

The town was established in 1762 along a trade route called Three Notched Road, which is the path of today's U.S. 250. It later became a rail hub, served by the Chesapeake and Ohio Railway and the Southern Railway, and the two lines crossed at a depot called Union Station.

Thomas Jefferson founded the University of Virginia, and the city is close to Monticello, Ash Lawn-Highland and Montpelier. Both Monticello and the university's Academical Village are UNESCO World Heritage Sites. Court Square is the original center of the city, and the Downtown Mall nearby is one of the longest outdoor pedestrian malls in the country.

For a seller, the practical point is that a house near the old core and a house in a later subdivision have different repair needs. We ask for the build year first because it guides what we look for during a walkthrough.

sections.h2: What does the economy mean for people selling a house in Charlottesville?
sections.html:
Charlottesville's job base leans heavily on the University of Virginia and its health system, along with city government, schools and research or finance institutions. The city's 2025 financial report places the University of Virginia, UVA Health Services Foundation, the City of Charlottesville and the City School Board each at more than 1,000 employees.

Other names in the top ten include ServiceLink Management at 500 to 999 employees, and Morrison Crothall Support, Albemarle County, ADP TotalSource and General Atomics at 250 to 499 each. The National Radio Astronomy Observatory headquarters, the CFA Institute and S&P Global have a presence in the area as well, and the unemployment rate was 3.1 percent in 2024.

Only about 18 percent of the people employed in Charlottesville live in the city. About 82 percent commute in, and 42 percent of those commuters come from Albemarle County. Meanwhile 11,497 city residents commute out for work. In plain terms, many people who hold jobs here live in the county, which is why a city seller competes with county houses for the same buyers.

  • More than 20,000 students come to the city for the university during the academic year, which affects rental demand near campus.
  • Two hospitals serve the area: University of Virginia Hospital and Martha Jefferson Hospital.
  • The Piedmont Virginia Community College has several locations in the city.

sections.h2: What is the climate like, and what should a seller watch for?
sections.html:
Charlottesville has a four-season humid subtropical climate, with hot summers, cool winters and rain in every month. July averages about 77.6 degrees Fahrenheit, January about 36.2, and the high passes 90 degrees on roughly 34 days a year.

Snowfall averages 17 inches a season, but it varies a lot from year to year and rarely stays on the ground for long. The wettest stretch is May through September. In terms of the house itself, that means air conditioning matters, attic ventilation matters and gutters have to handle summer storms.

  • Test the air conditioning and send in a service record if you have one.
  • Inspect the attic and the roof before listing.
  • Look at the ground around the foundation for erosion or pooling after storms.
  • Check the crawl space for moisture.

Virginia's seller disclosure form also tells buyers that the owner makes no statement about special flood hazard areas, dam break inundation zones, radon zones or marine clay soils. Buyers can ask for the information on their own, and a note from you about any past water problem builds trust.

sections.h2: How do people get around Charlottesville?
sections.html:
Interstate 64 and U.S. 29 are the main highways, with U.S. 250 and Virginia Route 20 also serving the city. I-64 runs east toward Richmond and west toward Staunton, and US 29 runs northeast toward the Washington area and southwest toward Lynchburg.

Charlottesville Area Transit provides city bus service, JAUNT runs paratransit vans, and University Transit Service covers the area around the university. The Charlottesville-Albemarle Airport handles commercial flights, and the Amtrak station is served by the Cardinal three times a week, along with daily Crescent and Northeast Regional trains. A Greyhound terminal is also in town.

For sellers, transit access can sharpen a listing. A house within walking distance of the Downtown Mall or a bus corridor appeals to renters and downsizers, while a house outside the core appeals to buyers who drive. We account for both when we price a cash offer.

sections.h2: Which public schools serve city homes?
sections.html:
Charlottesville City Schools run six elementary schools, Walker Upper Elementary School, Buford Middle School and Charlottesville High School. Albemarle County Public Schools serve the surrounding county and have their headquarters in Charlottesville.

If you are not sure whether your house is in the city or the county, the school system is one more clue. Some private schools with Charlottesville postal addresses are actually in the county, so a postal address alone does not settle it. Confirm the district with the school office before you tell buyers.

We could not open the city's own pages for rental rules, historic district review, zoning or the real estate tax calendar in time for this guide. Rather than guess, we recommend that you call the city's planning and building offices and the treasurer to confirm any local requirement before you list, rent or renovate.

sections.h2: What do sellers pay and sign in Virginia when a Charlottesville house closes?
sections.html:
Virginia imposes a grantor's tax on the seller, set at 50 cents for each $500 of the price, and the buyer and seller can agree in the contract to shift it. The tax is shared between the state and the locality, and the circuit court clerk will not record the deed until it is paid. The statute is at Virginia Code 58.1-802.

Unpaid real estate tax is a lien that outranks other liens, and the closing agent pays it from the seller's proceeds. The seller's share of the current year's tax is divided contractually. Read the lien statute at Virginia Code 58.1-3340.

You must also provide the Real Estate Board's residential property disclosure statement. The form states that the owner makes no representations on topics such as historic district rules, lot lines, adjacent parcels, flood hazards, easements, lead plumbing, drywall and the condition of any dam. Starting January 1, 2027, the statute adds an item about use-value assessment and roll-back taxes. Read the statute at Virginia Code 55.1-703.

sections.h2: How does a cash sale work for a Charlottesville seller?
sections.html:
A cash sale means the buyer does not need a mortgage, so the deal depends less on lender timing, appraisals and loan approvals. You contact us with the address and a few details, we review the house, and we make a written offer.

Owners in the city sometimes ask about selling a house they inherited, a rental that needs work, or a house they must leave quickly for a job change. We buy as-is, so you do not have to clean out the house or make repairs first. If the offer does not suit you, you owe us nothing and you can list with an agent instead.

This is general information about Charlottesville and not legal or tax advice. Check specifics with a licensed attorney or the local government.

faqs.a: No. Charlottesville is an independent city and the county seat of Albemarle County, but the two are separate governments. Your tax bill and address records show which one covers your parcel.

faqs.q: How many people live in Charlottesville?
faqs.a: The 2020 census counted 46,553 people. The Census Bureau's 2025 estimate is 44,388.

faqs.q: What does Virginia charge a seller when a deed is recorded?
faqs.a: Under Virginia Code 58.1-802 the grantor pays 50 cents for each $500 of the sale price, unless the contract moves some or all of it to the buyer. The clerk collects it when the deed is recorded.

faqs.q: Does Charlottesville get a lot of snow?
faqs.a: Snowfall averages about 17 inches a season, though it changes a lot year to year and rarely lingers, according to climate data on the city's Wikipedia entry. Summer is hot and humid, with about 34 days a year above 90 degrees.

faqs.q: Can I sell a house in Charlottesville without making repairs?
faqs.a: Yes. Virginia's disclosure form is built around the buyer doing their own due diligence, so you can sell as-is. You still give the buyer the Real Estate Board's disclosure statement.

faqs.q: Which airport and train station serve Charlottesville?
faqs.a: Charlottesville-Albemarle Airport handles commercial flights, and the Amtrak station is served by the Cardinal, Crescent and select Northeast Regional trains.
